claims.text: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has an interlaced microstructure containing at least two phases.
The constituent phases differ in corrosion reactivity and mechanical properties.
The initial alloy has a relatively coherent room-temperature oxide layer.
At elevated temperature, one eutectic phase oxidizes preferentially.
Preferential oxidation produces a brittle, poorly adherent, non-coherent oxide at phase interfaces.
Mechanical wear readily removes the fragile oxide.
Removal of the oxide exposes fresh susceptible metal.
The freshly exposed metal rapidly re-oxidizes.
Repeated oxidation, oxide detachment, and re-oxidation form a positive feedback cycle.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation of the more corrosion-active phase.
Oxide removal increases the effective wear rate by reducing surface integrity.
Repeated exposure of reactive metal increases the corrosion rate.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce an overall degradation rate roughly two to three times higher than the isolated baseline conditions.
Simultaneous exposure will cause degradation greater than the sum of the isolated wear and corrosion effects.
Simultaneous exposure will produce more pronounced pitting and non-uniform oxide formation than isolated exposure.
Simultaneous exposure will produce deeper and rougher wear tracks than isolated exposure.
The mechanism is expected to operate above approximately 500°C in oxidizing gas or molten-salt environments when the applied load is sufficient to remove fragile oxide scales.
The mechanism may not operate in alloys with uniform oxidation behavior or under lower-temperature or lower-wear conditions.

contradictions.description: The baseline and conditions describe wear-only testing at the same chemical environment as the corrosive test, whereas the falsification design specifies wear-only testing in an inert environment. These are not the same matched control and could yield different wear behavior.
